Adam: Damn.
*I appeared to have successfully damaged his shoulder, somewhat disheartened by the fact that an attack I poured all my strength into didn't particularly achieve anything significant. Still, I had no time to lament — Adam stood up.*
Adam: This sword isn't strong enough.
Setsuna: Agreed.
*One was a sword belonging to Archangel Michael, another to Archangel Uriel. A blasphemy if I'd ever heard one.*
*Still, they did indeed lack in sheer destructive power at present.*
*We cast our swords aside, and closed in on each other. I wondered if the tingling pain somewhere deep inside my nose came from fear, or from Adam's palpable killing intent.*
*Not like it mattered. Rather than pondering trifles, I should've thought of the most convenient and fastest way to crash my fist into his face.*
*I stopped. I should have probably come up with a strategy.*
The Two: AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAHHH!
*Succumbing to instinct, we proceeded to hammer each other with our fists. I threw a punch, and he responded with his own; ad nauseum. Our bout displayed a thorough lack of strategy or technique.*
*I hit him so hard I nearly dislocated my own shoulder. Yet each time my fist pounded his flesh, I felt elated.*
*And then he would hit me back. Every single time he'd touch me my entire body would fire up in furious agony as if pierced by a needle.*
Setsuna: Don't...
Adam: fuck with me!
*I hit him. My aching fists were seething, like they were on fire; my spinal cord felt cold as ice. My mind drowned in a maelstrom of pain and elation.*
*I got hit; my consciousness blacked out for a few seconds. Still, my basal yet stalwart fighting spirit helped recollect myself as I grounded my teeth again.*
*Our bout no longer displayed any elements of sportsmanship; it no longer had anything to do with martial arts, fencing, or even techniques of drunkards fighting with sticks.*
*We were hammering each other with nothing but fists, returning to the most primordial of states. Nothing commendable about it — just pure satisfaction on its basest level.*
*I acknowledged both his strength, and personality. And I believed him to have acknowledged me the same.*
*But we could never become friends. Or rather, we didn't want to. It was a notion that both of us felt inherently repulsed by.*
*I didn't feel malice towards Oshiba Hagane back when I fought him. I only felt sorry for him; I only wanted to put him out of his torment. Our relationship did come close to something akin to friendship in the end, I thought.*
*I felt nothing like that fighting Adam.*
*Whenever I'd look at him I'd be overtaken by an indescribable sensation; something akin to but not exactly killing intent, animosity, and an irresistible wish to fight.*
*My heart would go awry, robbing me of the ability to calmly analyze myself or my surroundings.*
*All I understood now was that he was trying to kill me, and that the thought made me very happy.*
*So I didn't hold back, and went for the kill myself. My cheeks were ruined by punches, my teeth were falling apart. I took a deep breath and blew it out, hindering Adam's vision with dust.*
Adam: ...!
*He was momentarily rendered blind. Without wasting another second, I landed a wild swing at his chin — a critical hit.*
*My triumph didn't continue for long.*
*Adam's right fist crashed into my liver.*
Setsuna: Ahh— Gahh—
*Its destructive power reaching the measure of tones, Adam's fist broke my ribs as if they were branches of a decrepit tree.*
Adam: Ah... Kh...
*Adam fell on his knees from pain, but his eyes still burned alive with almost palpable intent to kill me, his body trembling from sheer animosity.*
*I, too, was trembling and down on my knees, but this time it seemed my sheer fighting spirit — while able to cast pain and fear away — struggled to bring me back on my feet.*
*Still, I somehow managed to stumble back up. Our positions were the same as in the start — the sole difference was that we were now battered almost to death.*

*I cared only about one thing and one thing only — Adam, my nemesis.*
*The pain grew worse, my body heating up even further. It wasn't the most pleasurable of sensations, but the thought that my adversary had been suffering the same filled me back with elation.*

Adam: Tendou Setsuna, I live for Eve alone. I shall fight, and die for her. That's my raison d'etre.
*Adam declared his raison d'etre to me with pride.*
Adam: And you? Does your life belong to Kugutsu Sorami?
*I took a deep breath, and considered his words. _I wonder_.*
*I... certainly did not live only for myself. I lived for someone. For someone to be able to live in peace, with smiles and joy as their everyday.*
*Could I single out Sorami as the sole target of my aspiration? I... felt that wasn't necessarily the case.*
*So did I live then for the world? I didn't feel that to be the case, either. If I had to choose between Sorami and the world, I'd choose the former in a heartbeat.*

Setsuna: ...No.

Setsuna: Yeah.

Adam: It's about time we finished this.
Setsuna: Yes. The end is nigh.

*Your raison d'etre was something you had to grasp, and hold on to by yourself. Both in dreams, and reality.*

*Tendou Setsuna. What do you live for?*
*Adam. What do you live for?*
*I felt my cheeks caressed by a breeze that shouldn't have been there. Ah, we left the Gates of Heaven open; a gust might have sneaked inside.*
*Everything was so silent. Both the world outside, and the world within.*
*I couldn't even hear my own heartbeat.*
Setsuna: God of Thunder — Takemikazuchi!

Adam: Lend me your power, Emperor of Thunder — Raitei!

*Cutting through the air like bullets, our fists crashed into their targets with a thunderous bang.*
Setsuna: God of Might — Tajikara-wo!
Adam: Beast of Unrivaled Might — Behemoth!

Adam: My raison d'etre is to give my everything to my love.
Setsuna: My raison d'etre is to triumph over impossible odds with everything I have.

Setsuna: Wh—?!

*His shining heart let out a creak. The most robust part of the dragon body obeyed Adam's will and changed its shape to resemble that of a weapon.*
*A crimson blade made of his heart. The ultimate weapon that only the bravest could wield, for if it shattered, it would mean the end of its master.*
Adam: All of my power — all of myself, down to the very last cell — exists for her alone. And so I shall arm myself with the strongest weapon available to me.
*The world's most powerful sacred blade. The world's fastest demon sword. The world's most warped holy lance. And all the other divine relics in his arsenal.*
*He deemed them all worthless. In the end, the sole thing he had put his trust into was his very own heart.*
*A crystallized volcanic flame so potent one wouldn't hesitate for a moment before labeling it love.*
Adam: Erythro-Kardia, my crimson heart.
*Such was the weapon Adam chose.*
Setsuna: The world turns through the cogs of an intricate mechanism.
*And so I made my declaration. My power was such that I could triumph over impossible odds without relying on the saving grace of the divine.*

*And that made us despise each other. We felt repelled by, averse to, and positively loathed the very notion of being together.*
*And the reason for that was now clear as a day. For he was myself. The paths we walked differed, and so did the principles of our creed, but I still realized that he was but another possibility of my own self.*

*And he'd feel fulfilled. For such was her command.*
*But I couldn't let them have their way.*
*Maybe they were right, maybe their melancholic wish came from the very purity of their hearts.*
*But I still couldn't let them have their way. Despite everything.*

*We currently dwelled in the present.*
*The present that rested atop the foundation of the past. And if our present built upon that foundation it would eventually lead us to the future.*
*We always lived only to reach what lay beyond our current moment. We fought the present to attain the future.*
Setsuna: In order to suppress all adversity through devastating power...
Setsuna: I shall create God. I shall mold Him into being. That is my raison d'etre — Tendou Setsuna's reason for being!
Setsuna: I summon you, Universal Machine, Guardian Spirit of Time!

*Adam gave me a confident smile. And I couldn't blame him for it — the weapon I had summoned to overpower his turned out to be the exact copy of the very sword he held in his hands.*

*Sapphiro-Kardia, my azure heart.*

*While there might have been weapons that held more raw power by themselves, as long as this sword rested in the hands of a man with the strongest heart in the world — Adam — it would be unmatched.*

*I grasped her neck with my right hand, and while she was still in the midst of confusion, covered her lips...*

Sorami: Ah... Okay.
*Her cheeks still red, she nodded at me. I loved her with all my heart.*

Adam: I'll keep mine for later.
*Ah, that too wouldn't have been so bad.*
*Eventually, we took a step towards each other. And with it, I steeled my heart.*
*This sword required no tricks. It cut. And killed.*

*And so our hearts clashed. The world that Metatron had fashioned split in half with a deafening explosion.*

*The agony of having one's heart clash with another's was far worse than I had imagined.*
It wasn't only physical pain — I had long transcended that concept. It was worse: as our hearts clashed, we understood each other.
*I could now comprehend Adam thoroughly, down to the last detail. And he could comprehend me just the same.*
*Nonetheless, I would kill him. I'd reject my newfound feelings, and make him perish.*
*It was neither a strong conviction, nor a vague excuse like faith in God.*
*It was all for Eve. He would destroy the entirety of the world and everything therein because Eve wished so.*
*I vaulted up, swinging my blade downwards. He parried, knocking my sword out of its trajectory with tremendous strength. At the same time, he spun around and swung his sword at my side.*

Setsuna: Gh...!
Adam: Got you!
*But I didn't give up. As I felt my arm break, Adam let his guard down.*
*I planted a kick right in his face, and as he momentarily lost his vision, sent his own arm flying with a swing of my sword.*
*While one of us was regenerating his broken bones, and the other his severed arm, we both thrust our swords at each other's chest.*
*I gritted my teeth at the sensation of an alien object ravaging my chest. But I didn't die.*
*With our hearts in our hands, maiming our torsos amounted to little more than excruciating pain.*
*Still... at times, pain had the power to break hearts. We both seemed to share in that intention, yet neither of our hearts gave in.*
*With both of our left arms rendered useless, we ended up using our rights. I jumped forward, launching a ferocious thrust. A chop fell on me from above, likely with the intent to stop and counter my action.*

*The sole and only way to prevail was to break your foe's heart.*
*We tumbled down the white ground, rolling twice or thrice; he ended up atop me. Our arms regenerated at almost the very same moment.*
*His fist crashed into my face; at this point, I imagined he planned to grind it to minced meat.*
*Unnerved by the grotesque thought, I launched my own fist up towards the sky. His cheekbone shattered, while I spit out my own teeth.*

*We kept landing hit after hit on each other in a neverending rondo of fists.*

*Adam, not bothering to wipe the blood off his face, continued to glare at me.*
*His unadulterated love was likely the strongest feeling known to this world. He probably loved Eve more than I could ever love Sorami.*
*And so, I couldn't hope to win in terms of affection. Realizing that, I couldn't help but let out a chuckle. What a way to lose.*
*In the end, I couldn't become a hero. Those who fought for love would always win. The myths of mankind stood testament to that — as long as the hero had someone he loved at his side, he always prevailed.*
*And the source of all of Adam's power was, without doubt, exactly that.*
*Each time we clashed, the world around us ripped apart. It wasn't because it was poorly made; the world Metatron created had been as heaven-like as the original.*
The reason was simple: not even the divine realm could withstand the destructive power of our weapons.
Adam: ......
*Confusion manifested on Adam's face. Enduring the impulse to vacate my stomach, and wiping the sweat out of my eyes, I smiled to myself — I knew what had perplexed him.*
*His heart brimmed with love for Eve. And that affection was what gave him his power, so potent it tore the world apart*
*I, on the other hand, was nothing like him. I loved Sorami, I truly did. But I also knew full well that I couldn't compare with the passion of _his_ affection.*
*My love wasn't pure. I didn't love Sorami herself, but rather the future that was waiting for me with her.*
*And I didn't love Sorami alone; I loved everyone. My heart was fliled with love, almost like it was running a bargain sale on affection.*
*It wasn't that hard to overcome the fear of death. Overcoming torment, on the other hand, was no such easy task.*
*Knowing it wasn't the best of ideas, I cut most of the pain signals coming to my brain, relying only on my sense of touch.*
*My fear waned, and my fighting spirit shot up.*
*How could I overcome the fear of death that easily?*
*The answer was simple — I knew I wouldn't have a long life ahead of me either way.*
Naru: Three years? Maybe two if you exert yourself too much.
*I recalled her saying something along those lines. I wasn't designed for posterity; my vitals would likely stop one day without as much as a warning.*
*I'd be overcome with fear whenever I considered the idea. Despite the terror, though I couldn't shake off the thought. I simply couldn't stop thinking about it.*
*At times I thought I'd make peace with my fate, and look death straight in the eye. While I had been afraid of becoming a god as well, the fear of death overshadowed it by a large margin.*
*A bout of death that nobody could ever hope to interfere with at this point.*
*The sky split apart. The world shattered to pieces like glass. The remnants of the old heaven peeking out from beyond the destroyed layers.*
Setsuna: ...!
Adam: Shyaaah!
*I missed my swing, and was flung away by the counter that followed. My bones had cracks and hairline fractures all over at this point; my regeneration powers could no longer keep up with the damage.*
*My heart continued to shoot blood through my veins; I had all of my nanomachines concentrate solely on regeneration.*
*Still, it wasn't enough. To tell the truth, it was a miracle in itself that my arms and legs were still attached to my body.*
*I couldn't get up. Even though I wished to — with all my heart —, my body refused to obey my will.*
Setsuna: Ah... Gh...
*All I could do was wail, unable to even form words.*
*Adam landed nearby, looking down on me with a detached expression.*
Adam: And so, it all ends now.
*He clutched his sword with both of his shaking hands. His own heart, Erythro-Kardia.*
*Love was a powerful force. In the end, no one could best it.*
*Nonetheless, I refused to yield. I had no idea how much of my life span I still had left, but even if Sorami had ordered me to destroy the world, I wouldn't have listened.*
*The world was a far more fascinating place than I had ever imagined. It was neither a kind, nor a particularly harsh place. Despair had no control over the world, for if people tried hard enough, hope could always be discovered.*
*I wished to preserve such a world — as a final present to her before my death.*
*Both of our hearts were already littered with cracks. I stifled my fear, ignoring the pain. I refused to cry and give in to terror.*
*If I yielded here, the world would surely fall. And so would Sorami, together with our future.*
*He sent me flying with another merciless kick, shattering the last of my ribs.*
Naru: The world is cold as ice.
*She said that once, and I agreed. The world had always been cold, unforgiving, and filled with cruelty.*
*Nonetheless, I yearned to live. I yearned to be a part of this world.*
*My only wish had been to entrust my dreams to this world. To feel its beauty.*
Setsuna: Ah.
*I saw a vision of a future together with Sorami.*
*A soothing sight, illuminated by the beautiful orange of a sunset. But one detail in that picture surpassed even its majestic glow.*
*The smile on Sorami's face.*
Setsuna: Ah... Ahh—
*Tears welled up in my eyes as blood trickled down my lips. I couldn't allow this scenery to remain a lie — an illusion.*
*_Stand, Tendou Setsuna_. _Stand, and ready your sword one last time_.*
*_Perish in a battle waged for the sake of the future_.*
Setsuna: AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAHHH!
*I swung my sword with a howl, still prone. Adam jumped back —evading the swing —, and brandished his own sword.*
Adam: You still have some fight in you...?!
Setsuna: Of course I do!
*I brandished my sword as well. Lights colored azure and crimson danced in unison.*
*Space itself got torn apart, with everything around us being flung down to the nether. The rift separated us like a demarcation line.*
*We hesitated for a second — we both understood the next attack would likely prove to be our last.*
*I discarded all cognitive thoughts, and instead left everything to the instincts of my trusty partner over the past few years — my own body.*
*Little by little, the vacuum that had formed between us dissipated.*
*It felt as if the whole world had been flooded with some viscous liquid; the air itself seemed _dense_.*
*Somewhere in the depths of my consciousness I realized I howled. I realized I jumped forward.*
*Without interference from my mind, my body moved as it saw fit while I kept the sword of Sapphiro-Kardia tightly in my grip.*
*I lifted it up to the sky. And swung it downward.*
*With my mind dormant, I took less than a second to aim. My body moved reflexively as I entered his sword's reach.*
*I didn't care about what Adam was doing. So I wasn't particularly unsettled by the fact that our swords clashed again.*
*There was no use lying anymore.*
*Adam smiled to himself. Little by little, cracks started appearing on his weapon — and with it, on his own heart as well.*
*He must have known this would happen.*
*Destroying the world probably wasn't that hard a feat for Adam at this point. And if I lost, he would doubtless proceed with the plan, and succeed in a heartbeat.*
*But he knew that wish wasn't _right_.*

Samael: Ahaha, thank you for everything, really. And prepare yourself!

*Persian Zoroastrianism was also a great influence since they liberated them from their captors.*
*Finding solace in their religion, Hebrews grew to believe that it was their fate to one day return to their lost homeland, and rebuild the destroyed temple of Jerusalem.*
*Eventually, that belief came to incorporate afterlife, where another Jerusalem — one in Heaven — would rather welcome them instead.*
*The idea of men entering Heaven was later reinforced by the stories of the righteous Enoch and the prophet Elijah who had entered their Lord's kingdom while they were still alive (The Book of Genesis, and The Book of Kings of the Old Testament respectively).*
*It is likely that the story of Adam and Eve, and their exile from Paradise after having consumed the forbidden fruit was also related to the Hebrew wish to return home.*
*In any case, Heaven — that used to be just a dwelling place for God and his servants — had became a paradise that promised eternal bliss to the ancient Jews.*
*Various stories depicting Heaven, Hell, and the prophecies of the end of the world — the so called apocalyptic literature, like the Book of Daniel — began emerging in the second century BCE.*
*Among them, the apocryphal Second Book of Enoch that depicts the righteous man visiting seven heavens after his ascension is particularly telling of the idea of Heaven that Jews had just before the emergence of Christianity.*
*The Merkahab Riders was a school of early Jewish mysticism that immortalized their ideas in what is now called Hekhalot literature.*
*They believed that abstaining from food and commitment to meditation would summon a divine chariot that would take them through the seven heavens to God's Throne.*
*In the case of Christianity and the New Testament, only in the Book of Revelation is there a brief description of God's Throne and its surroundings.*
*In the fourth century AD, however, various priests and religion scholars appointed by Saint Augustine had many discussions about the nature of Heaven.*
The fruit of their endeavors was such: that churches and the cities that contain them on earth were all just a reflection of the grand Jerusalem above the skies.
*The understanding of Heaven by those of Catholic faith was more or less summed up in the fourteenth century by a distinguished poet by the name of Dante Alighieri in his masterpiece "The Divine Comedy."*
*The Heaven depicted in the work is a toric world coiling around the Earth.*
*A sphere of fire separates the Earth from the moon, and after it extend ten layers of Heaven.*
*The first eight carry a name and serve their respective planets, while the ninth layer holds the whole power of the divine.*
*The tenth — the Empyrean — is the ultimate dwelling place of the Holy Mary — the empress of Heaven —, her servant angels, and the saints.*
*Angels that are divided into nine ranks each belonging to one of the three triads, play music in the Empyrean, where, surrounded by nine divine lights, God sits on his throne.*
*Hell is a place where the souls of sinners go to receive their punishment after death according to Christianity. It has many different depictions, varying greatly among the various literature; there are even schools that deny it altogether.*
*It is thought that it was about 4000 BC when humans first started exploring the theme of life after death.*
*The oldest currently known depiction of the world of the dead was found in The Epic of Gilgamesh where it was understood as a place separated from the world of the living by a vast river, and existed far under the ground.*
*In ancient Egypt, the world after death was ruled by the god Osiris, where a dog-headed god, Anubis, weighed the hearts of the dead with his scales of justice to tell their worth.*
*The understanding of the underworld in ancient Greece was highly influenced by the Egyptian myths, where a god Hades ruled over the depths of Earth — Tartarus — and had a three headed hellhound guard its entrance.*
*The progenitor of Christianity, Judaism, however, never possessed a complicated depiction of an after world, only having a place called Sheol where all dead regardless of their past deeds gathered and rested.*
*Sheol means both "grave" and "hole" and has been thought to be somewhere underground.*
*Meanwhile, Gehenna, which developed into the modern interpretation of hell was a place where apostates of Moloch sacrificed their children to their god. Also known as the Valley of Hinnom, historically it was also used to burn trash and dead bodies.*
*As already mentioned in the entry on Heaven, an event called Babylonian Exile had a major effect on Jewish understanding of the world, which made their depiction of hell change significantly during their captivity and the rise of the Apocalyptic literature.*
*In the apocryphal Book of Enoch written around the second century BC, the hell where sinner's souls were gathered (Gehenna) is located in the third stratum of the seventh layer of Heaven.*
*While there is also a paradise in the third stratum where angels live in peace, in its northern section that is hidden by darkness and mist there is a burning river that flows down into a valley which the angels of punishment cast sinners and fallen angels into.*
*The spartan image of God in Jewish faith pre-dating Jesus Christ is reflected in the Old Testament where there is a hell in Heaven, and it is angels who participate in the torturing of sinners.*
*With the birth of Christianity in the first century AD, Hell was moved down underground, functioning as a kind of prison where not angels but the devil Satan (or Beelzebub, or Belial) and his servant demons tortured the sinners instead.*
*In an apocryphal work of Christian folklore, the "Gospel of Nicodemus," Jesus Christ visits Hell after being crucified, and capturing Satan, presents him to the underworld's true master, Hades.*
*Incidentally, in the Roman Catholic faith, there is also another area neighboring Hell called "Limbo."*
*It is a place whose purpose is to house those waiting for the day of salvation.*
*Denizens include priests from the times before the crucifixion of Jesus Christ, children that died unbaptized, and other criminals whose sins weren't as heavy to warrant going to Hell.*
*The current Christian understanding of Hell originates mostly from the fourteenth century epic poem "The Divine Comedy" by Italian poet Dante Alighieri.*
*In the Divine Comedy Hell is a conical-shaped hole in the land of Israel.*
*It leads up to the very center of Earth, and consists of nine circles.*
*In the deepest layer of the ninth circle, Judecca, a three headed devil with humongous wings, Lucifer (Satan), stands stuck with his lower half frozen in ice.*
*He keeps cursing the names of three traitors — Judas Iscariot, Marcus Junius Brutus, and Gaius Cassius Longinus — shedding tears from all six of his eyes.*
*Purgatory is a relatively new concept that first appeared in the canon of Roman Catholic Church after its split with the Eastern Orthodox Church.*
*Aurelius Augustinus was a fourth century priest who created the foundations for Christian theology.*
*He argued that people who haven't committed any grave sins, but weren't particularly good in their lives either, should first go through trials to wash away their impurities before being allowed into Heaven.*
*The concept of "Purgatory," a place where the souls of the dead would be purified by fire, and also a general name to define a divine trial, was raised as an answer to this issue.*
*It was added to the canon of the Catholic Church in the twelfth century to stress the transience of power in the mortal world in feudalistic Western Europe.*
*Just like Heaven and Hell, the modern image of Purgatory was heavily influenced by the fourteenth century Italian poet Dante Alighieri and his masterpiece "The Divine Comedy."*
*Under the guidance of the ancient Roman poet, Publius Vergilius Maro, Dante finds his way through the nine circles of Hell, and discovering a hidden path in its deepest layer, emerges in the southern hemisphere of Earth.*
*On the very opposite side of the planet from Jerusalem, he finds himself in an island where a terrible mountain rises into the sky. There he meets an old man who calls himself Cato overseeing the mountain of purgatory.*
*Turns out, his full name was Marcus Porcius Cato Uticensis (Cato the Younger) who worked as a tribune in the Roman times of Julius Caesar.*
*Dante also spots two angels with flaming swords in the sky, seemingly observing the Purgatory from there.*
*Beyond the Peter Gates guarded by an angel with an unsheathed sword, lies seven circles of Purgatory.*
*They each correspond to one of the seven deadly sins — Pride, Envy, Wrath, Sloth, Greed, Gluttony, and Lust.*
*Angels inhabiting those circles work to purify humans of their sins, and lead them to the paradise of eternal spring at the very top of the mountain.*
*The seven deadly sins, also known as the capital vices, is a classification of vices that has been used since early Christian times to educate and instruct Christians concerning fallen humanity's tendency to sin.*
*Originally not a part of the Biblical canon, the idea gained popularity after a fourth century Egyptian theologian, Evagrius Ponticus, came up with eight evil thoughts that most plagued mankind — gluttony, fornication, avarice, hubris, sorrow, wrath, vainglory, and sloth.*
*In the sixth century, Pope Gregory I revised this list to form the more common seven deadly sins.*
He melded sorrow into sloth, vainglory into pride, and adding envy, ending up with: gluttony, lust, greed, sloth, wrath, envy, and pride.
*In the Purgatorio of Dante Alighieri's "Divine Comedy," the purgatory is divided into seven circles each corresponding to one of the deadly sins.*
*Particular sinners are purified in these seven circles of their transgressions.*
*As the demonology grew more prominent in the sixteenth century, seven deadly sins were conjoined with particular demons.*
*The first such instance is recorded when a painter and woodcut printmaker, Hans Burgkmair, prepared ribbons with inscriptions of seven deadly sins.*
*He drew demons on their name plates to denote their sin.*
*While in the seventeenth century play "Doctor Faustus" by Christopher Marlowe, seven deadly sins make an appearance in the form of demons.*
*A German theologian, Peter Binsfeld, described what sins which demons liked the most in his writings on demon classification published in 1589.*
Pride: Lucifer
Envy: Leviathan
Wrath: Satan
Sloth: Belphegor
Greed: Mammon
Gluttony: Beelzebub
Lust: Asmodeus
*The entrance to Heaven that is described as a ladder in the Book of Genesis of the Old Testament.*
*Jacob was the blessed grandson of prophet Abraham who later receives the name of Israel, and becomes the progenitor of all of the Hebrew race.*
*On his way to visit his uncle in Haran, he spends a night camping in the wilderness near the town of Luz, and sees a dream of angels traveling from Heaven to Earth and back via a giant ladder that pierced through the sky.*
*As he stands dazed by the stunning sight, God appears next to him, and informs him that this land would be his from now on.*
*Turns out, Jacob slept at the very place where the entrance to Heaven was located.*
*Jacob makes a pillar out of the stones he used for a pillow, and names that land "Bethel" — "House of God."*
*This Bethel later becomes a sanctum for the Northern Kingdom of Israel.*
*The apocryphal Testament of Jacob offers more information about this ladder.*
*The ladder is made of twelve steps, and on each step there are two human forms, one on each side of the step, visible as far as their breasts.*
*According to the angel Sariel, those twelve steps symbolize the number of eras of mankind, and the faces on them belong to the most prominent heretics of that time.*
*In the Book of Daniel of the Old Testament, it is also mentioned that among the seventy Ethnarchs — angels responsible for protecting countries — only Michael, the guardian angel of Israel, didn't forsake God.*
*In relation to that, there is some folklore explaining that the guardian angels of Babylon had to ascend 70 steps, those of Media 52, those of Greece 180, and those of Rome even more.*
*Samael, as the guardian angel of Rome, has to climb so many steps he rises above the clouds, claiming himself to be almost as good as God to Jacob, but soon ending up punished for his impudence by the Lord.*
*It was likely the influence of Babylonian mythology and Zoroastrianism that led to the idea that angels needed hierarchy.*
*Proof of this is named angels like Michael and Gabriel suddenly appearing in the Jewish writings of the sixth century BC, particularly the Book of Isaiah of the Old Testament.*
*The hierarchy of angels grew together with the Christian society that was separated into different classes under the philosophy of Plato.*
*It was the book of Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite "On the Celestial Hierarchy" that influenced it the most.*
*In a way, it was used as a political tool to justify the inequality in society in medieval Europe while the church preached equality of men.*
*Angel ranks in the "On the Celestial Hierarchy" are named after words that come up in the Bible and related literature in relation to angelic and divine forces.*
*Their ranks are seraphim, cherubim, thrones, dominions, virtues, powers, principalities, archangels, and angels.*
*These are further divided into three hierarchies, spheres, or triads.*
*The first sphere angels serve as the heavenly servants of God the Son incarnated.*
First Rank: Seraphim
*Literally translated as "burning ones," Seraphim are the highest class of angels.*
*They are said to encircle God's Throne, existing off the love emanated by God, and unceasingly chant the Trisagion, "Holy, holy, holy...".*
*This burning love keeps them ever close to the throne and they bear love and light to the lesser choirs of angels.*
*Their six wings are a symbol for their ability to ascend as far to Heaven as God.*
Second Rank: Cherubim
*Characterized by a deep insight into God's secrets, the cherubim hold the knowledge of God and possess the entirety of the divine science of Heaven.*
*It is also they who are often sent to earth with the greatest of tasks.*
*They enlighten the lesser choirs of angels and are to them the Voice of Divine Wisdom.*
Third Rank: Thrones
*The primary function of these angels is to be God's chariot but they are also noted as meting out God's judgement. Their main characteristics are submission and peace, however they act with impartiality and humility to bring about the desires of the Lord.*
*Angels of the Second Sphere work as heavenly governors of the creation by subjecting matter and guiding and ruling the spirits.*
Fourth Rank: Dominions
*They rule over all the angelic orders charged with the execution of the commands of the Great Monarch.*
*They act as a form of middle management between the upper choir and the lower.*
*Receiving their orders from the seraphim and cherubim these bright spirits make known to mortals God's commands and ensure the cosmos remains in order.*
Fifth Rank: Powers
*The favorites among mortals, they hold one of the most dangerous tasks, maintaining the border between Heaven and Earth.*
*Constantly on guard for demonic attacks, the powers act like an elite guard.*
*They are appointed in a special way to fight against the evil spirits and to defeat any wicked plans.*
Sixth Rank: Virtues
*They maintain the aspects of the natural world, and to bestow blessings upon the material world.*
*Angels who function as heavenly guides, protectors, and messengers to human beings.*
Seventh Rank: Principalities
*They guide and protect the world's nations, towns and cities, directly watch over the mortal world and are executive in regard to the visible world of men.*
Eighth Rank: Archangels
*A term or title normally used to describe important or special angels, but here is used as the second to last rank in the celestial hierarchy.*
*Archangels serve as guardians of great personages, and are also charged with overseeing the duties of the angels.*
*The confusion about the collective celestial rank of archangels arises from the ancient Hebraic way of defining angels which was simply angel and archangel.*
*The hierarchy was defined until much later, and many of the angels previously named as simply archangels were given new posts.*
Ninth Rank: Angels
*They are the ordinary messengers sent to men to watch over mortals in a more direct manner than the principalities.*
*According to the teachings of Christianity, one day the souls of the dead will rise from their graves, and Jesus of Nazareth (Christ) will return to earth.*
*It would prove to be the day of last judgement, when the sins of all mortals would be weighed, with those exalted rising to Heaven, and those condemned cast to Hell to suffer for all eternity.*
*The interpretations of the last judgement vary from school to school, with Roman Catholics for example calling it the Day of Reckoning.*
*In the end times, the souls and bodies of the dead would rise from their graves regardless of the sins they committed in their lives.*
*For souls and bodies are irrevocably intertwined, and to receive the last judgement from God, they would have to face Him together.*
*During the last day, it is also said that Jesus Christ would fight and defeat the forces of evil with Satan at their helm in the Battle of Armageddon.*
*Armageddon apparently refers to the Megiddo mountains located in the northern Israel.*
*Most of the information about Armageddon comes from the Book of Revelation of the New Testament, though in truth it alludes to at the time still young movement of Christianity fighting, and defeating the Roman Empire that persecuted their faith.*
*That, among many other reasons, led to a split in Christian community as to how they interpret the concept of Armageddon.*
*Some sects believe that it all already happened and passed sometime in the first century AD.*
*Others believe the battle itself happened but the judgement and the return of Jesus have yet to come to pass.*
*Lastly, a select few believe everything would still occur in the far future.*
*It is thought that the concept of Armageddon was heavily influenced by a very similar notion of the end of the world in Zoroastrianism.*
*Saoshyant, the final savior of mankind sent by the absolute benevolent god Ahura Mazda, would come to earth and battle the wicked led by the seed of all evil Angra Mainyu.*
*After the victory of the forces of good, stars would rain down from the sky, and on the scorched lands dead would rise again and be exalted.*
*A "night monster" or "night hag/witch" that appears in Jewish mythology. Her name is thought to be connected with the Semitic word "LYL" meaning "night," but there are also theories that she holds her heritage to storm spirits.*
*She is only mentioned once in the Bible, in the Book of Isaiah, describing the desolation of Edom, where the Hebrew word "lilith" appears in a list of eight unclean animals.*
*Lilith as a spirit that approaches men with malicious intent, however, appears in the Dead Sea Scrolls as "the seductress," and is mentioned multiple times in the Babylonian Talmud.*
*An interesting theory states that a female monster "ki-sikil-lil-la-ke " that appears in the oldest surviving piece of literature "The Epic of Gilgamesh" is actually the precursor to this Jewish demon.*
*In the Jewish folklore from middle ages Lilith is regarded as Adam's first wife, and later as a wife of Satan (Samael).*
*In the first chapter of "Genesis" it is written that God made both a man and a woman in his image, however, in the second chapter he creates another woman for Adam — Eve — who is for some reason treated as a single man again.*
*This passage gave rise to the idea that Eve was actually Adam's second wife.*
*The legends of Lilith are more or less summed up in the anonymous medieval text (VIII-XI century) "Alphabet of ben Sirach."*
*Refusing Adam's wish to only have sex in missionary position, she leaves her husband and ends up living at the coast of the Red Sea, where she has relationships with many demons and gives birth to countless children called "Lilim."*
*In response God sends three of his mighty angels — Senoy, Sansenoy, and Semangelof — to her.*
*He also threatens to kill a hundred of her children every day she refuses to come back to Adam.*
*Lilith then drowns herself in the Red Sea, and turns into an evil spirit that hunts and kills Adam and Eve's children instead.*
*In the thirteenth century Kabbalistic text of two brothers Isaac and Jacob Hacohen, other than being the wife of Adam, Lilith is said to be one androgynous being with Samael that corresponds in the spiritual realm to Adam and Eve who were likewise born as a hermaphrodite.*
*Raziel is an archangel within the teachings of Jewish mysticism who has recorded all knowledge known to Earth, as well as all the disasters that would befall mankind in her book called Sefer Raziel that she presented to Adam and Eve.*
*Her name means "Secrets of God," and so she is a keeper of all mysteries that pertain both to Heaven and Earth.*
*There are two legends as to how her book ended up in Adam's hands. One where the original man gets it before the exile from Eden, and the other after.*
*According to the former, Samael visits Eve in Eden while Adam is away, and asks her to look over his son.*
*As Adam comes back, he is unable to stand the wailing of the child, and he ends up killing it out of irritation. Still, even after death, it continues to keep crying, and so Adam, after closing its mouth, devours it together with Eve.*
*All of it being just a trap of Samael — his so called son an evil spirit — the devoured being ends up assimilating with Adam's heart, as Samael tells him it will remain in the body of mankind forever, inherited from father to son.*
*To help Adam out of this predicament, God presents him with Sefer Raziel where the treatment of the curse is inscribed.*
*According to the latter legend, answering the prayers of Adam and Eve who wander around earth clueless of what to do, Raziel appears before them and presents them with her book to give them worldly knowledge. (In case of Kabbalah's Zohar it is Raphael who appears before them instead.)*
*Sefer Raziel goes missing after Adam's death, but through a revelation in a dream, Enoch discovers it again, and learns from it his divine knowledge.*
*It is also said that Noah built his ark according to the design inscribed in Sefer Raziel that Raphael presented to him.*
*Passing through the hands of Abraham, Jacob, Levi, Moses, Joshua, and finally King Solomon, it disappears from history once again.*
*Ancient Jews would carry small books with Raziel's name on them in their pockets, or would keep them under their pillows as a good luck charm.*
*In all religions that treat the Old Testament's Torah (The Five Books of Moses) as canon — Judaism, Christianity, Islam — Adam is the name of the first man created by God.*
*According to "Genesis" God has gathered dust from the surface of the earth, shaped it into the image of himself, and breathed in it life through its nostrils.*
*Adam, as a common word in the Hebrew language, means "human," but it is also thought to be related to the word "adamah" which means "ground" or "earth."*
*There is also a theory that the name comes from the son of the god Set of Egyptian Mythology — Edom (meaning "red man").*
*According to the Talmud, which is also a part of the canonical scriptures of Jewish faith, God made Adam's body out of clay, and called him golem, before breathing life into him.*
*In the Jewish mysticism, golems are dolls made out of mud or earth that a rabbi would infuse with life to make them their servants.*
*Using the Talmud as reference, a French scholar, M. Henrion, calculated that Adam, who was described to be so tall as to reach the canopy of the sky, was 134 feet (41 meter) in height.*
*God created Paradise in Eden that was supposedly at the eastern edge of the world for Adam to dwell in, and then fashioned one of his ribs into a woman.*
*A woman, however, seems to be created twice in the first two chapters of Genesis, which led many to speculate that Adam had another wife before Eve, and in the later Jewish folklore she came to be known as Lilith.*
*According to the Talmud, Adam was looked over by angels in Paradise, where they would indulge him in all sorts of worldly pleasures, like cooking meat or serving cold wine.*
*Satan, however, — at the time still an angel serving God — grew envious of their comfortable life.*
*In "Life of Adam and Eve" — an apocryphal book of Old Testament — and Quran — the holy book of Islam — Satan (Iblis in Quran) refused God's orders to serve Adam, and so was exiled from Heaven.*
*Later, Adam and Eve, too, are exiled from Paradise for eating the forbidden fruit of knowledge.*
*In most writings it is believed that the snake that tricks Eve is another form or a servant of Satan (Samael, Lucifer).*
*Even though God punished them for their transgressions, his love for his children hadn't vanished, and he continued to help Adam and Eve by having his servants Raziel and Raphael teach them about how to survive on earth, and help them in other ways.*
*According to "Life of Adam and Eve," once the first two humans passed away together, four angels — Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, and Uriel — descended from Heaven, and buried them in the earth, at the same time teaching Adam's son, Seth, about the proper ritual burial.*
*The first century BC philosopher, Philo of Alexandria, interpreted The Five Books of Moses as a moral lesson, and calling the travails of Adam in the book of Genesis as a symbolic journey to strengthen and lead the man's soul to ultimate heavenly form of Adam Kadmon (original man).*
*The concept was later adopted to many schools of Jewish mysticism, including Gnosticism, Manichaeism, and Kabbalah.*
*Within the Kabbalah, Adam Kadmon is a perfect androgynous hermaphrodite that functions as part of God's very body.*
*The Tree of Life that is especially important in the teachings of Kabbalah (Tree of Sephiroth) shares the same symbol with the body of Adam Kadmon.*
*Meanwhile, the mortal Adam grew to be called "earthly Adam" to separate him from his perfect self in Heaven.*
*Eve is the name of the woman that God creates out of Adam's rib in the Book of Genesis of the Old Testament.*
Adam, who had to name all of the living beings on earth, gave her that name (Hebrew: Hawwah) to commemorate her as the "Mother of all the Living."
*Her name shares the root with the Hebrew word "haya" that means "to live."*
*Hawwah is also an alternate name for the ancient Ugaritic goddess Asherah, the wife of one of the greatest of Babylonian gods, Anu, who even makes an appearance in the Old Testament, and is thought to have at one time been worshipped as the consort of Yahweh by the ancient Jews.*
*It is believed that the original motif of Eve has been borrowed from other legends common in the land of Canaan.*
*It is primarily from a myth about the Sumerian goddess Ninhursag who creates and lives in a beautiful garden.*
*Her name can relate both to "rib" and "life" (the Sumerian word "nin").*
*It has been a common practice to assimilate other gods into the religion before the composition of the Old Testament.*
*In the Book of Tobit that is treated as deuterocanonical by Roman Catholics, and apocryphal by Protestants, it is mentioned that God created Eve to "assist" Adam.*
*One can see a reflection of the patriarchal social system of the ancient world in the scriptures about the first two humans.*
*Eve in her ignorance gets tricked by a serpent to eat the fruit of knowledge in her husband's absence, and ends up having them both exiled from the paradise.*
*In Gnosticism, the feminine aspect of God ends up giving birth to Pistis Sophia Aeon (an angel) after attaining forbidden knowledge, and in her passion for her masculine aspect also gives birth to an artificial god Yaldabaoth (creator god).*
*One can see many parallels between this, and the story of Adam and Eve in the Book of Genesis.*
*The story of the two original humans itself, however, is turned upside down within the gnostic belief, as the serpent who tricks Eve — a woman created by the fake god Yaldabaoth — supposedly works under the orders of the true God in gnostic scriptures.*
*Unlike Samael, Belial, and Azazel who later got converged under the single name of Satan, Astaroth is mentioned as a separate god of the heathens in the Old Testament.*
*The name first comes up in the Book of Job as the name of the capital city of Bashan Kingdom situated on the east side of The Sea of Galilee.*
*It is believed that a god by the name of Astaroth has been locally worshipped in the land of Canaan before Hebrews moved into it during the time of The Book of Judges, and that the capital city of the Bashan Kingdom boasted a temple for the deity.*
*As the first king of Hebrews, Saul, loses a battle against the Philistines in The Book of Samuel, it is mentioned that his enemies placed his armor as a sacrifice in the temple of Astaroth.*
*There was a time when the younger generation of Hebrews, forgetting the miracles of God that saved their people in the times of the Book of Exodus, had taken to worshipping the local deities of Canaan — Astaroth, Baal, and Asherah — as well.*
*The young men were most likely tempted by the sexual rituals, where the sacred prostitutes would please the participants as a part of the holy rites.*
*God, in response, struck everyone with disease and famine that would eventually restore the faith in him, but none of his attempts seemed to last, as after a while people would end up going back to their pagan ways again.*
*The third king of Israel, Solomon, brings his country unprecedented prosperity, but at the same time, tempted by his foreign wives, ends up worshipping Astaroth, Molech, and Chemosh that results in the kingdom splitting apart.*
*The king of the southern part of Israel Kingdom, that comes to be known as Judah, among his many reforms obeying the wisdom of the Book of Deuteronomy he was said to possess, also destroys a temple to Astaroth that Solomon had built in Jerusalem.*
*It is commonly thought that the veneration of Astaroth/Astarte in Canaan originated from the widespread reverence of the Mesopotamian goddess of fertility, Ishtar.*
*This goddess of many loves and passions even makes an appearance in what is regarded as the first great work of literature "The Epic of Gilgamesh."*
*The goddess becomes infatuated with Gilgamesh after hearing of how he vanquished the monstrous forest guardian Humbaba with his friend Enkidu.*
*She offers to marry the two-thirds god one third-human of Uruk, but he refuses.*
*The young hero states that she has ruined all her other lovers in the past by betraying them as soon as she got bored.*
*Offended by the truth, Ishtar sends the Bull of Heaven to ruin the lands of Uruk, but Gilgamesh and Enkidu promptly kill the beast, for which the gods punish Enkidu with death.*
*In John Milton's epic poem "Paradise Lost," Astaroth makes an appearance as a heavenly goddess with a crescent-shaped horn on her head, as Satan summons all demons in hell together. His interpretation was likely heavily influenced by Astaroth's past as the fertility goddess.*
*The legend was still unknown in the times of John Milton, but in the Ba'al Epic of Ugarit, a new goddess by the name of Ashtart takes the place of Ba'al in the divine hierarchy and briefly rules over the heavens before getting exiled.*
*It is highly possible that Ashtart and Astaroth were the same deity in the Old Testament.*
*In middle age Europe, Astaroth was made into a demon, and in the eighteenth century magical book "The Grand Grimoire," is listed as one of the rulers of Hell together with Lucifer and Beelzebub.*
*In the Hierarchy of Demons by Johann Weyer that became the basis of the Lesser Key of Solomon, Astaroth is listed as a duke of hell with forty legions of demons under his command who guards various treasures.*
*In most books of demonology he is illustrated as holding a poisonous snake in his right arm, and riding a beast of hell that looks like a dragon. He is depicted as a fallen angel who has unbearably bad breath.*
*Astaroth, being a part of countless different mythologies and fields of study, perfectly illustrates the common practice and process of assimilation of foreign gods to fallen angels or demons in the Bible.*
*First appearing in the Jewish folklore, but much more prominent in Kabbalah, Camael is the master of one of the ten sephirots that leaked from God as he created the universe — "Gevurah" symbolizing the "Strength of God."*
*Within Kabbalah he is also sometimes called Kemuel.*
*According to the foundational work of Kabbalah — Zohar, Kemuel (Camael) is the commander of twelve thousand angels of destruction, and is charged to guard the gates of heaven.*
*The angels of destruction are angels whom are bid to rain carnage and diseases on earth to punish the sinners. They are sometimes likened to the "God's Sword" as a symbol of divine punishment.*
*They are the ones responsible for the destruction of the depraved cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, and have once completely annihilated the whole Assyrian army in a single night. Uriel is also sometimes listed as their leader.*
*Kemuel's name can also be interpreted as "assistant" or "the meeting of God," and within the teachings of Gnosticism he is labeled as an archon of seraphim.*
*However, in spite of his incredible power, Kemuel meets a frightful end in one of the tales of Jewish folklore.*
*At one time, a single man visits the gates of heaven, and insists that he has done so with the permission of the lord himself.*
*Out of his iron sense of responsibility, Kemuel ends up refusing the suspicious man from passing, but ends up killed as the conflict with the visitor escalates into a fight.*
*It was Moses, one of the most prominent prophets of Hebrew people, that came to the gate.*
*In the Book of Exodus of the Old Testament, Moses receives orders to free his people and lead them to the promised land of Canaan from God on Mount Horeb, but there also exists a legend that Moses didn't just receive God's message, but visited heaven itself at the same time.*
*Incidentally, in Zohar, Kemuel lets Moses pass, but despite offering to accompany the prophet on the way, gets rejected as only Moses was ever told the real name of God.*
*In 1946 there have been found a collection of ancient religious texts in the Qumran Caves on the northern side of the Dead Sea in the Arabian peninsula.*
*Now termed as "Dead Sea Scrolls" these writings are thought to have been left behind by an Essenes sect of Judaism who lived a relatively secular life in the area.*
*This Qumran Sect identified Satan, who was imprisoned in the desert for rebelling against God (Mastema), as Belial.*
*The term "belial" is a Hebrew adjective meaning "worthless," and since first appearing in the Book of Samuel of the Old Testament, has been likely adapted to refer to demons.*
*In the War Rule scriptures of the Dead Sea Scrolls, an army of the Sons of Darkness commanded by Belial clashes, and gets destroyed by the Sons of Light — the Qumran Sect.*
*In the later ages, unlike Samael, Mastema, and Azazel who were converged into the concept of Satan, Belial was always treated as an individual, independent demon.*
*In the Middle Age Europe, Belial was treated as a silver tongued jurist of hell, and many of the writings from that age note that most theological ideas would be tested in the court of Belial and Jesus Christ.*
*In the "Book of Belial" (Liber Bellial) published in 1382 by Jacobus de Teramo, Lucifer sues Jesus Christ for having trespassed by descending into Hell. King Solomon presides over the court, while Belial is the counsel for the Devil.*
*With Moses as Jesus Christ's counsel, and his opponent, Belial loses the case, and the son of god is cleared of charges.*
*In exchange, however, the Devil is granted the right to take possession of the bodies and souls of the damned at the day of the Last Judgement.*
*The idea of Jesus Christ fighting a legal battle against Belial most likely stems from a line in chapter six of the "Second Epistle to the Corinthians" (Letter A) — "And what concord hath Christ with Belial?".*
*In the seventeenth century, Belial grew to symbolize debauchery and corruption.*
*John Milton, a strong proponent of the puritan movement, later described Belial as the worst and most despicable of the fallen beings who loved evil for evil's sake.*
*He made him show up last in Satan's court in his epic poem "Paradise Lost."*
*It is likely that Milton tried to express his dissatisfaction with the court of Charles II and the London citizens of the time who didn't obey puritan values.*
*In the Lesser Key of Solomon, Belial is numbered 68th, while in Johann Weyer's Pseudomonarchia Daemonum he is ranked 23rd.*
*To force the truth out of deceptive and tricky Belial one had to make him swear to tell truth and only truth under the lord's name.*
*Otherwise, you will get overwhelmed by his silvery tongue, and the boundless capacity for lies.*
*Emerging to the physical world on a burning chariot as an angel of beautiful voice and appearance, Belial has the power to improve your standing in society, expedite your friendships, and prepare you with capable servants.*
*In the Lesser Key of Solomon it is mentioned that Belial is a commander of eighty legions of Powers and lesser angels, but in its English version, there is a note, that he only had fifty legions with him, left by the English magician Aleister Crowley who published the book.*
*Heavily influenced by John Milton, the novelist Victor Hugo left behind works like "The End of Satan" and "God" after his death.*
*Deciding to live in exile after Napoleon III's coup d'etat, he also wrote a book titled "Toilers of the Sea" where the inhabitants of the French coast all thought that demons had their ambassadors in all countries of the world. Belial was responsible for Turkey.*
*Also sometimes called Dantalian.*
*In the Book of Kings of the Old Testament, the third king of Jerusalem, Solomon, is depicted to have learned the secrets from either God himself or his angels, and used them to bind demons to his power in the temple of Jerusalem.*
*In the late middle age grimoire the "Lesser Key of Solomon," that describes all 72 of Solomon's demons, and the ways to summon them, Dantalion is introduced as the 71st.*
*The grimoire itself is based on another grimoire written in 1577 by a Dutch physician and a strong critic of witch-hunts, Johann Weyer, "Pseudomonarchia Daemonum."*
*Originally an appendix to another writing, "Book of the offices of spirits," it, too, lists 69 demons, but Dantalion is not among them, indicating that he was likely a new addition in the Lesser Key of Solomon.*
*Dantalion is described as a grand duke who leads 36 legions of spirits.*
*The appearance of Dantalion is disputed and vague, as in the Lesser Key of Solomon he appears as many people, both male and female.*
*There is a possibility that he was used to explain multiple personality disorders. In most of his depictions, he holds a book in his right hand, and instructs those that summon him on arts and sciences.*
*What makes him terrifying, however, is not his extensive knowledge.*
*According to the Lesser Key of Solomon, he knows the thoughts of all men and women, and can change them at his will.*
*He can also create various illusions of people and visions, and unleash them unto the world according to his summoner's wishes.*
*Dantalion is a demon responsible for the will and knowledge that men possess. He might be especially relevant in the modern day society of information.*
*Allegedly first appearing in the sixteenth century's (most scholars now believe it was actually written in the early 19th century) book on demonology "The Grand Grimoire."*
*He is also known as "The Red Dragon," Lucifuge Rofocale literally translates to "he who feels from light" from Latin.*
*In his 1599 work "Magical Investigations," a Jesuit theologian Martin Delrio argues that Lucifuge is a term used to describe all demons that are afraid of light.*
*According to the Grand Grimoire, the three masters of hell — Lucifer, Beelzebub, and Astaroth — also had six highly ranked spirits to serve them as their chancellors, that include Baal, Agares, Marbas, and Lucifuge.*
*Lucifuge Rofocale is responsible for overlooking wealth and treasures, and can bring riches by forcing other demons into signing contracts that are to their disfavor. He provided services very much relevant to the modern world.*
*In the sixteenth century grimoire ascribed to the legendary king Solomon who purportedly used demons to build the Jerusalem Temple, "The Lesser Key of Solomon," there is a demon named Focalor listed as 41st in the ranking.*
*Seeing how it is an anagram of Rofocale, it is likely that Focalor is an alternate name for Lucifuge, and if not, then it at least has deep ties with the latter.*
*Focalor is a Great Duke of Hell, commanding thirty legions of spirits. He has power over wind and sea, and works to sink ships, killing people by drowning.*
*It is mentioned that he had hoped to return to Heaven after one thousand years of service to King Solomon, but was deceived in his hope. From this inscription, one can assume he, too, used to be an angel like Lucifer.*
*Lewis Spence assigns Lucifuge the rank of Throne before his fall.*
*A very unique angel appearing all throughout the Jewish folklore.*
*An eternal trickster who on one hand defies God and spreads evil all across the world, and on the other follows his divine decree to collect the souls of the dead, as well as to report the sins of mortals to the divine court.*
*While within Christianity the title of Satan is usually ascribed to Lucifer, in the scriptures of Judaism it is usually Samael who is seen as the Devil.*
*Samael's name translates to the "Poison of God," and there is an interesting theory that suggests it might be related to the eastern god of fear, Samana.*
*The poison of Samael refers to the fruit of knowledge because of which Adam and Eve ended up being banished from paradise.*
*In the Book of Genesis of the pseudepigraphal Jonathan translation of the Bible it is Samael who tricks Eve into eating the fruit.*
*Among some of the apocryphal scriptures of the apocalypse literature it is also mentioned that he taught the two original humans the taste of wine.*
*Many of the evil deeds related to snakes — Satan — in the Old Testament are ascribed to Samael in the later writings.*
*His trick with his son, mentioned in the entry on Raziel, was probably just a variation on the fruit of knowledge story.*
*Samael is depicted in various ways depending on the literature, sometimes with twelve wings, sometimes with all of his body covered in eyes, and sometimes as a giant black hound.*
In the Zohar ("Radiance") of Kabbalah, the four angels of sacred prostitution: Lilith, Agrat bat Mahlat, Eisheth Zenunim, and Naamah, are Samael's wives.
*As a servant of God, Samael is also known as the angel of death.*
*His function was similar to that of the grim reaper in ancient Judaism, where he would inform people about impending death, and reap their souls, taking them with him down to Sheol (underworld).*
*The angel of death, however, wasn't treated as an evil spirit, as even Michael and Metatron are sometimes ascribed to that role.*
*Samael, as an angel of death, appears in the stories related to the death of the prophet Moses.*
*As Moses frees Jewish people from slavery, and leads them through the desert to the promised land of Canaan, some of his followers sin in losing faith in God, and Samael is the one to descend and inform him of his fate to die without reaching his destination.*
*As Moses comes closer and closer to Canaan, he starts praying to God that he would allow him live a few more years in the promised land, but Samael does everything in his capacity to thwart his prayers.*
*According to the Talmud, it was also Samael who informed Heaven of Moses' death.*
*However, seeing the death of his brother Aaron mourned by all 24,000 thousand of his followers and countless angels, Moses, too, ends up wishing for the same end, and gouges Samael's eyes out as he descends to reap his soul.*
*Samael, however, keeps obsessing with Moses' soul, and in the currently lost apocryphal scripture of the Old Testament "Assumption of Moses" is said to have contended with Michael over the possessive rights of the prophet's body.*
*Despite being God's servant, Samael was self-centered, and loved causing chaos on the surface of the earth which led him to many fights with his fellow angels.*
*Among them, Sandalphon was particularly averse towards the chaotic angel, and it is said that countless wars have been waged among the two.*
*According to Jewish folklore, however, only Metatron and Akatriel know of a way to defeat Samael.*
*There is a legend of eighteenth century theologian Rabbi Yisroel ben Eliezer summoning Samael, and asking him to show him and his pupils the true face of God.*
*Samael, being tormented by the constant desire to punish sinners and burn cities, asks the rabbi to tell him the names of a couple of sinful cities in exchange for his deed.*
*One of the seven archangels, the vigilant Uriel is responsible for overlooking the boundless abyss, Tartarus, at the deepest layer of Sheol.*
*Tartarus is the prison for those that fought the current gods in ancient times in Greek Mythology, and is more or less equivalent to what Jews called "Gehenna."*
*With the rise of Christianity, Hell became the territory of the demons imprisoned there, but in the times before it was mostly agreed that angels ruled over the underworld as well.*
*Uriel means "Flame of God" or "God is my light," and is usually depicted as having his right hand lit in divine flames.*
*Many theologians believe that "Flame of God" is actually a metaphor for lightning.*
*Uriel, despite not appearing in the canonical books of the Bible, is constantly mentioned with Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael in apocryphal and pseudepigraphal writings, ending up being known as a distinguished angel nonetheless.*
*In the pseudepigraphal scripture of "Life of Adam and Eve," Uriel along with the other three master angels buries the bodies of Adam and Eve, and teaches their son Seth the proper rites of burial.*
*In the apocryphal Book of Enoch of the Old Testament, Uriel wields thunder and terror, and together with Michael scours through the rubbles of earth devastated by the giants called nephilim born of a union between men and angels, reporting his findings to God.*
*In the First Book of Enoch Uriel shows Enoch the way to God as he enters Heaven as a living man.*
*In the Fourth Book of Esdras, he guides the prophet Esdras as he prays to understand God's divine plan — in the apocryphal writings Uriel is pictured as a loving angel of guidance.*
*Within Christianity and Judaism, however, he is usually understood as an angel of punishment.*
*Uriel is sometimes thought as one of the angels of destruction who punish Hebrews and their enemies for their transgressions in the Old Testament.*
*Meanwhile, in the canon of the Roman Catholic Church he is sometimes treated as a fallen angel.*
*The ten commandments that God bestows upon Moses explicitly forbid any form of idolatry.*
*Yet as the religion expanded and absorbed many followers from different faiths there arose a need for sub-gods to ease them into the church.*
*For example, Michael was sometimes thought of as Mercurius (Hermes in Greece).*
*Eventually, however, many areas started worshipping all sorts of angels local to their territory.*
*As a response, in 363 or 364 AD, the church summoned the Council of Laodicea and came to a decision to forbid veneration of any angels other than Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael.*
*These were the only angels explicitly mentioned in the canonical scriptures of the Bible.*
*Meanwhile, the Council of Rome in 745 AD, seven locally worshipped angels were abolished of their divine status for descending on earth and impersonating saints. Among them was Oliver, an alternate name of Uriel.*
*In the seventeenth century epic poem depicting the war between angels and demons by John Milton titled "Paradise Lost," Uriel is an angel responsible for the light of the sun.*
*According to Milton, neither humans nor angels can see through the lies of fallen angels, and so Uriel gets tricked by Satan who takes the shape of a cherub (an angel with wings) after escaping from Gehenna, and tells him the whereabouts of Adam and Eve.*
*Hearing his words, however, Satan momentarily resumes his original horrid shape out of envy for the two humans, and Uriel then seeing through his disguise, promptly informs Raphael, the leader of guardian angels, of Satan's incursion.*
*Appearing in the Book of Biblical Antiquities, Gethel is one of God's angel servants.*
*After rebelling against the injustice of Pharaoh's rule, Moses receives the ten commandments directly from God.*
*He then flees Egypt together with his Hebrew brethren.*
*After his death, Joshua steps up to continue leading his people to the promised land of Canaan, and as he presses onwards, he runs into many hostile tribes local to the area.*
*One of them were the Amorites that dwelled in the lands of the Middle East since before the twentieth century BC.*
*At one time, one of the Hebrew leaders, Cenez, in his recklessness, decides to attack an army of Amorites with a very small force.*
*Seeing his hopeless venture from Heaven, God sends two of his angels to help Cenez.*
*One of them is Gethel (or Ingethel), who rules over the hidden things, and worketh unseen, and another an angel of might, Zeruel.*
*The two help Cenez with their powers.*
*Gethel smites the Amorites with blindness, so that every man that saw his neighbour counted them his adversaries, and so they slew one another. Meanwhile, Zeruel strengthens the weapons of Cenez and his troops lest the enemies should still somehow perceive him.*
*This was how Cenez, through the intervention of unseen angels, managed to defeat an army of twenty thousand Amorites with minimal force.*
*The Book of Biblical Antiquities, usually ascribed to a person commonly termed as "Pseudo-Philo," is a collection of short stories and legends inspired by the Old Testament.*
*These range from the making of the world to the rule of the first Hebrew King, Saul, and many other apocryphal and pseudepigraphal scriptures.*
*It is an exceedingly important document shedding much light on the ancient Jewish folklore.*
*In one of its retellings of The Book of Judges, an angel who appears before the parents of the hero Samson who grows to fight Philistines for Jewish people, and informs them of his conception.*
*He is named Phadahel — a name previously unknown to Jewish lore.*
*An angel that makes an appearance in the seventeenth century poet John Milton's masterpiece "Paradise Lost."*
*His name meaning "a servant to God," he used to be a subordinate of the angel of light Lucifer (Satan).*
*There was a rumor that the name of Abdiel comes up in the Middle Age grimoire "Sefer Raziel," but it since has been discredited, proving him to be John Milton's original creation.*
*He is the only one of the commander angels under Lucifer who expresses absolute indignation at his master's attempt to revolt against God, and splits with him as the latter seduces about one third of Heaven to fight against God in John Milton's "Paradise Lost."*
*Being the first to report Satan's rebellion to God, he promptly joins the army led by Michael and Gabriel, and inflicts considerable losses to Lucifer's army by soon felling Ariel, Arioch, and Remiel in battle.*
*One of the most memorable scenes from "Paradise Lost" is when Abdiel laments as he witnesses that Lucifer has retained his beautiful shape and dignity despite the fall, but fights his once master nonetheless.*
*In the later literature, however, he has been assigned to some quite unexpected roles; "The Revolt of the Angels" of the twentieth century writer and Nobel laureate Anatole France being one of the most memorable examples.*
*As Abdiel descends to earth as a human, he strives to look for a key to answer the secrets of God and Creation in mortal literature.*
*He eventually comes upon Gnosticism which depicts the Jewish God as different from Christian.*
*Here he is labeled as an evil fake deity, Yaldabaoth (the son of chaos), who was responsible for creating the world and its master — Archon.*
*His suspicion about creation might have stemmed from Lucifer's words in "Paradise Lost" where he declares that angels weren't made by God.*
*Learning the truth, Abdiel returns back to his old commander Lucifer, and instigates another rebellion against God.*
*A high ranking angel appearing in Jewish folklore pertaining to the birth of Metatron.*
*His name meaning "The Branch of God," according to Sefer Hekhalot ("Book of Palaces").*
*He is the keeper of the key to the palace of Arabot where God's Throne is located in the seventh heaven.*
*He is also counted as one of the eight angels of Merkabah (God's Chariot), and is a master of water and the secrets of Heaven.*
*In Sefer Hekhalot, Anafi'el descends down from Heaven on a chariot pulled by horses of fiery flames, and, in front of everyone, seats the righteous Enoch into it, and rises with him back to the divine domain.*
*Blessed by God, Enoch turns into the archangel Metatron, gaining the position of Chancellor of Heaven — the highest among the known angels. He also grows to be known as "Youth" or "Small YHWH."*
*However, to the very end, Anafi'el is kept depicted as a being above Metatron.*
*In truth, Sefer Hekhalot lists some other never before heard angels who are supposedly even higher than Anafi'el (and so Metatron) in rank.*
*At one time two rabbi, Akiva ben Joseph and Ishmael Ben Elisha visit Heaven while still alive (both lived at around two century AD).*
*Spotting Metatron being served by other angels, Elisha exclaims that there are two gods in Heaven.*
*Hearing that, God orders Anafi'el whom everyone was afraid of in Heaven, to give Metatron 60 "strokes with fiery rods" to punish him for his impudence.*
*In one of the Kabbalah's scriptures titled "Hekhalot Rabbati," Anafi'el is one of the six angels guarding the palace on the seventh heaven, and is given the title of the master of Israel, as Anafi'el YHWH.*
*Interestingly enough, there is another Anafi'el listed as the guardian of the palace on the fourth heaven in the same scripture.*
*According to the apocryphal Book of Enoch, Remiel, his name meaning "Mercy of God" (also sometimes called Ramiel or Ramuel), falls in love with a mortal woman and descends to earth.*
*He later becomes one of the leaders of the fallen angels (as Ramuel).*
*But in the Greek version of the same scripture, he is also listed as one of the seven vigilant guardians of God, and is responsible for looking over those that God had resurrected.*
*In John Milton's Paradise Lost, Remiel is depicted as a violent rebellious angel that gets defeated by Anafi'el.*
*In the pseudepigraphical Syriac Apocalypse of Baruch, that depicts prophet Baruch starting to hear the voice of God after witnessing the destruction of Jerusalem's Temple by the hands of the Babylonians, Remiel has an important role.*
*At one time Baruch, the supposed author of the Book of Jeremiah, sees a vision of a cloud arise from the sea and rain down twelve times alternately dark and bright waters.*
*After these twelve waters comes another water still darker than the others and shot with fire, carrying annihilation in its wake.*
*Then a clear flash puts an end to the fearful tempest.*
*Appearing as a messenger from God, Remiel then explains to Baruch that the six dark waters are the dominion of the godless — Adam, Ancient Egypt, Canaan, Jeroboam, Manasseh, and the Chaldeans.*
*The six bright waters stand for Abraham, Moses, David, Hezekiah, Josiah, and the time of the Second Temple.*
*Finally, he explains that dark cloud itself is the period between the time of the Second Temple and the advent of the Messiah that would determine the dominion of the wicked, and inaugurate the era of eternal bliss.*
*In the Book of Kings of the Old Testament, Remiel is an angel who annihilates the whole army of Assyrians in a single night during their conflict with Judah, the Southern Kingdom of Israel.*
*According to the Apocalypse of Baruch, Remiel, hearing out the prayer of Hezekiah, the king of Judah, descends upon the nightcamp of Assyrians.*
*He then scorches the 18,500 commanders and 34,225,000,000 of their soldiers to dust, that only their armor and weapons are left lying vacant on the desert.*
*An angel that appears in much of Jewish folklore, and Kabbalistic scriptures, according to some he is one of the seven angels closest to God.*
*There is much controversy regarding the etymology of Metatron's name, but the theory of "one who serves behind the throne" (meta thronos) is the most widely accepted one.*
*The identity of Metatron is closely related to the mystifying sentence from Genesis 5:24 "Enoch walked with God, then he was no more, because God took him."*
*This made many theorize that the righteous man Enoch — great-grandfather of Noah and seventh generation grandson of Adam — ascended into Heaven to become an angel.*
*While most of the more modern stories about Enoch stem from the apocryphal Books of Enoch (1 Enoch, 2 Enoch of Old Testament, and Apocalypse of Paul), in the ancient times he was most well known as the "scribe of justice" who visited the palace of God as a living man.*
*Around the fifth century AD the idea of Enoch becoming Metatron gained popularity, and the book that cemented it was the sixteenth century Kabbalah scripture the "Book of Palaces" (also known as 3 Enoch).*
*In the Second Book of Enoch, the scribe ascends to Heaven carried on the wings of two angels, Raguel and Sariel.*
*In the Book of Palaces, it's the angel Anafi'el that performs the same task.*
*As Enoch reaches Heaven, God gives him a new name of Metatron, presents him with 10 graces, and blesses him with 1,365,000 blessings.*
*Then, he transforms Enoch's flesh into fire, increases his size to that of the width of the world, and fixes onto him seventy-two wings each of which could cover the whole earth.*
*He also turns his eyes to flashes of lightning, covers his shoulders with a magnificent mantle, and presents him with seven gems that shine in such radiance they lit up Heaven.*
*Finally, he places on his head a crown on which He inscribes his secret name with his own hand.*
*Furthermore, he makes angels ready another throne in his own palace on the seventh Heaven for Metatron to sit in.*
*Calling Metatron "Small YHWH," God makes sure all angels know about the stature of their new master.*
*The highest ranking angels like Gabriel and Remiel admire Metatron for his power, and even Samael — who is thought of Satan in the scripture — shivers from fear at his magnificence.*
*According to Jewish folklore, even among the angels, only Metatron and Akatriel have enough power to defeat Samael.*
*Metatron has seventy different names in all countries of the world, and being relatively young among the angels is sometimes referred to as "The Youth."*
*According to legends, Metatron is the one to inform Egregori — angels that descended down to earth infatuated by mortal woman — of the incoming flood, and their arrest (that was the role of Enoch in the First Book of Enoch).*
*Metatron is also thought to be the one who has led Moses from Mount Horeb to Heaven.*
*Metatron looked out for his children, Israelites, supporting King David and Zerubbabel among many others from the shadows.*
*He is also sometimes thought as a twin being to the angel Sandalphon, a sworn enemy of Samael, and in some apocryphal scriptures is even mentioned as his brother.*
*Sandalphon, just like Metatron, was originally a human — prophet Elijah — before ascending to Heaven.*
*In the Book of Kings of the Old Testament, Elijah was a prophet who participated in many battles against the heretics, purging the apostates of the God of Storms Baal in the land of Canaan, and raining fire and brimstone upon the army of Moabites who revere Baal-Zebub (Beelzebub).*
*In one of the passages of the Book of Kings, a chariot of fire pulled by fiery horses descended in front of Elijah, and with a gust of wind, took him together with it to Heaven.*
*A terrifying hellhound that guards the boundary between Earth and the Underworld, Styx River, so that the souls of the dead couldn't escape Hades in Greek mythology.*
*Its concept stems from ancient Egypt, where dogs were thought of as the protectors of graves.*
*In Theogony — an eighth century BC poem by Hesiod describing the origins and genealogies of the Greek gods — the beast is described as a son of Zeus' nemesis Typhon and the half-woman half-snake being Echidna.*
*Originally it was conceived as a monster with fifty heads, with a voice of bronze (hoarse).*
*He was, however, later reconceptualized as a huge dog of only three heads, with a mane and the tail made of snakes. Sometimes he was also drawn as a lion.*
