*He is the younger brother of the two-headed black hound Orthrus that is slayed by Hercules.*
*Cerberus had many heads to note that while some were sleeping, others were awake, and so explain why he could guard River Styx indefinitely, without a moment's rest.*
*However, if he hears beautiful music, slumber overtakes him, and all of his heads can fall asleep at the same time.*
*Orpheus — a musician that rushes to the Underworld as a living man to rescue his lover Euridike — uses his harp to put Cerberus to sleep and pass unnoticed.*
*There is also a legend that the beast loves anything sweet, and that one could pass through him if he offered him cakes or bread soaked in sop (sweet alcohol).*
*In the medieval books of demonology he reemerges as a devil Naberius.*
*In the "Lesser Key of Solomon," Naberius is described as a black crow, rooster, pigeon, or crane. In the "Infernal Dictionary" by Jacques Collin de Plancy he is depicted as a crow with two dog heads dressed in noble attire.*
*He has a raucous voice but presents himself as eloquent and amiable. He makes men cunning in all arts (and sciences, according to most authors), but especially in rhetoric.*
*In the Book of Job of the Old Testament where God tests the faith of one of his most loyal believers, the righteous Job, with most rigorous of trials prepared by Satan, Leviathan is mentioned as a sea monster that God destroyed in the past.*
*In the Book of Psalms of the Old Testament, God splits the sea apart, and crushes Leviathan's head to dust, feeding his carapace to sharks.*
*Leviathan, or Livyatan in Hebrew, means "twisted, coiled."*
*Leviathan and another sea monster Rahab, are commonly likened to Lahamu that the primordial goddess Tiamat gives birth to in the fight against the heroic deity Marduk in Mesopotamian mythology, indicating that they were assimilated to the Bible from older stories.*
*There is another sea monster that was used to symbolize raging seas in Ugarit mythology in the land of Canaan — Lotan.*
*In the Book of Genesis of the Old Testament, it is mentioned that during the fifth day God creates monsters of the sea.*
*But in the Christian version of Genesis, there appears to already have been a primordial sea of chaos ruled by the giant dragon Leviathan before genesis, which God had to suppress before creating the world.*
*Later rationalists theorized that Leviathan might be a word for a whale, but from the mentions of scales in the Book of Job, it is currently believed the legend stems from ancient people meeting with crocodiles in the Nile river.*
*Apart from Leviathan and Rahab, a monster by the name of Behemoth is also mentioned in the Book of Job.*
*All covered with tough muscle, Behemoth boasts incredible strength, not even raging whirlpools could make him give ground.*
*His bones made of bronze, his limbs as iron pillars, his skin tougher than armor rendering all thorns of the natural world impotent, he lives hidden deep among the reeds of swamps.*
*In the Jewish folklore he was thought of as a land mass equivalent to Leviathan, and in the sixth chapter of the apocryphal Book of Enoch, it is mentioned that Leviathan who dwells in the sea, and Behemoth who dwells in the desert, were split apart during the fifth day of creation.*
*In the Middle Age Europe it grew common to liken the entrance to Hell to Leviathan's mouth.*
*In the sixteenth century when demonology grew particularly popular with countless grimoires being printed, Leviathan grew to be thought of as another fallen angel who rebelled against God.*
*The concept was likely related to another story in the Jewish folklore, that talked about Rahab (who was thought as Leviathan) as a guardian angel of Egypt who tried to interfere with the Jew's escape from Egypt in the Book of Exodus.*
*The seventeenth century French inquisitor Sebastien Michaelis argues that all demons are fallen angels in his book "Admirable History," and lists Leviathan, Lucifer, Beelzebub, and Asmodeus as the highest ranking fallen angels.*
*Meanwhile, German theologian Peter Binsfeld conjoined Leviathan with the deadly sin of Envy.*
*In the grimoire "The Book of Abramelin" Leviathan is listed as one of the four princes of Hell along with Lucifer, Satan, and Belial.*
*In his book "Leviathan" seventeenth century political philosopher Thomas Hobbes, argues that a life without government, a condition he calls the state of nature, would lead to a "war of all against all," and likens the utopia of absolute monarchy to Leviathan.*
*It is quite interesting how Hobbes formulating his ideas in the midst of Puritan Revolution that eventually led to the execution of the king, Charles I, as a royalist, had to flee the country.*
*Likewise, John Milton, a supporter of democracy, who suffered from royalty as monarchy was later restored, ended up mocking England under the rule of Charles II likening it to Leviathan in his "Paradise Lost."*
*One of the three angels that appears in the canonical scriptures of the Old Testament, his name literally translating as "who is like God."*
*There is a theory that during the exile period, as the Neo-Babylonian Empire made Jew intellectual elites leave their homeland and move into Babylon as per orders of Nebuchadnezzar II, Jews have assimilated one of the gods local to Chaldea area into their religion as Michael.*
*Some scholars believe that the guardian god of Babylon, Marduk, or the god of Zoroastrianism, Mithra, might have been the inspiration for Michael.*
*In the Book of Daniel of the Old Testament where Michael first makes his appearance, it is mentioned that among the seventy Ethnarchs — angels responsible for looking over countries — only Michael, the guardian angel of Israel, didn't forsake God.*
*As Archistrategos of all angels, Archangel Michael has always been a special figure in Jewish mythology, and always figures as one of the seven angels closest to God, despite there being various contradicting lists changing the positions of other angels.*
*He is called "Holy Michael, the Archangel" and treated as a saint within Christianity.*
*The most prominent adversary of Michael and his angel armies, is the fallen angel Satan, who, abandoning God, caused disasters on earth in Judaism, and fell from grace due to pride and envy in Christianity.*
Within Judaism, Satan is a conglomerate of three devils: Azazel, Samael, and Belial.
*In the apocryphal Book of Enoch, Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, and Uriel descend to earth to capture the fallen angels who descended upon earth infatuated by mortal women.*
*Michael also has a fight with Samael over the rights to possess the prophet Moses' body.*
*In the Book of Revelation of the Old Testament, Michael leads the army of angels to fight Satan and his legion of rebellious angels.*
*Michael, after a long battle with Satan who takes the form of a giant red dragon, shackles his adversary with unbreakable chains, and imprisons him in the boundless abyss.*
*In the apocryphal "Life of Adam and Eve," Michael and Satan have a huge fight regarding God's order to serve and revere Adam whom God created in his own image.*
*It was probably the moment that Michael and Satan stopped seeing eye to eye.*
*According to Catholics, angels were created on the first day of genesis, all at the same time.*
*However, according to the New Testament apocrypha, "Gospel of Bartholomew" depicting the life of one Jesus Christ's twelve disciples, God first created Belial out of a fistful of fire (also known as Sataniel), and then made Michael second.*
*According to the teachings of the religiopolitical sect of Bogomilism that appeared in Bulgaria in the 10th century AD, Satan who had lost his divine title (el meaning God) is the first of God's children, and is thought of as Michael's (who is Jesus Christ) older brother.*
*It was likely the influence of this legend that made Satan and Michael appear as brothers in much modern fiction.*
*Michael is also responsible for listening to mortal prayers, and guiding the souls of the dead to Heaven.*
*There are many depictions of Michael holding a sword, a spear, and scales in his hands.*
*He is also sometimes depicted with wings ladened with countless eye looking patterns, reminiscent of the tail of a peacock, that is probably the influence of the Book of Revelation which mentions that high ranking angels, like seraphs, are all covered in eyes.*
*In the Qur'an of Islam, Mikail (Michael) is thought of as the second angel in rank after Jibril (Gabriel).*
*His magnificent wings are vividly green ladened with saffron yellow feathers in the local legends.*
*Each of those feathers have a million faces on them that chant the praises of Allah in a thousand of words.*
*Only the angels Gabriel, Raphael, and Michael are ever mentioned by name in the canonical books of the Bible. The three are also always listed among the seven angels closest to God.*
*Except that the Book of Tobit where Raphael makes an appearance, is excluded from the canon of Protestant faith.*
*Gabriel, whose name means "God is my power," is the angel who informs Holy Mary of her pregnancy with Jesus Christ.*
*On the other end of this peaceful image, Gabriel was also an angel of war.*
*In the apocrypha of the Bible, Gabriel is the one to look over Eden after the exile of Adam and Eve, and the one to annihilate the Nephilim giants who were born of a union between mortals and angels.*
*Gabriel also makes an appearance during the final battle of the epic poem about Charlemagne's (Charles the Great), the legendary king of Franks, nephew and the leader of twelve paladins, Roland.*
*Gabriel presents the holy sword Durandal to Charlemagne, and leads him and his army to victory against the muslims.*
*Raphael, whose name means "God Heals," is the protector of mortal souls, and healer of ailments.*
*In the Book of Tobit of the Old Testament, Raphael appears in the form of a man in front of the Jews Tobit and his son Tobiah in the town of Nineveh.*
*He then binds the demon of lust, Asmodeus, who plagues the daughter of their relative, Sarah, in the town of Media.*
*The story ends with Raphael guiding Tobiah and Sarah to marriage.*
*Raphael always appears as a very good-natured and well-meaning angel in Jewish folklore.*
*In the Zohar of Kabbalah, Raphael is the angel who recovers the Sefer Raziel that Adam lost, and is the one to present it to Noah as he builds his ark.*
*A legendary beast from European legends, known as the king of snakes.*
Its outward appearance is different depending on the literature: sometimes it has the body of a chicken with giant wings, that has a tail of a snake, sometimes it is a giant eight legged lizard with a head of a rooster.
*The interpretations of the beast have changed significantly in the long time it was present in local folklore.*
*According to the Naturalis Historia of a Roman philosopher Pliny the Elder, the basilisk of Cyrene (currently Eastern Libya) was a small snake, "being not more than twelve fingers in length."*
*Unlike other snakes, the Basilisk does not move by wriggling but from the center forwards to the right. It has a crown-shaped white crest on its head, and is so venomous that its gaze alone can prove lethal.*
*One could identify the habitat of the basilisk by the surrounding vegetation being burnt by the deadly venom it leaves in its trail.*
*To exterminate the beast, one should place a beast in the hole leading to its nest.*
*Leonardo da Vinci later figured that the beast in question should be a weasel.*
*The Basilisk also appears in the late fourth-century Latin translation of the Bible (The Vulgate).*
*In the Book of Psalms he is one of the monsters, with lions and dragons, that God (Messiah) tramples under his feet. In other words, the beast was associated with demons since very old times.*
*It was later merged with another mythical beast from European legends, cockatrice, attaining even more mystifying properties.*
*Apparently, it is born if a hen's egg is hatched by a snake or a toad.*
*Everyone who meets its gaze turns into stone, but if you have a mirror, you can reflect its gaze back at the beast, and turn it into stone itself.*
*In the fourteenth century story collection by Geoffrey Chaucer, the beast makes an appearance by the name of basilicok.*
Ouroboros (ancient Greek: "tail-devouring snake") is depicted as a serpent or dragon eating its own tail.
*It first appears in the Enigmatic Book of the Netherworld, an ancient Egyptian funerary text, as an illustration of two serpents, holding their tails in their mouths, coiling around the head and feet of Ra, the God of Sun, as the manifestations of the deity Mehen (uraeus cobra).*
*The holy uraeus cobra is a guardian deity that coils around the sun to protect it against the giant serpent Apep, born of the watery abyss Nun. It is a motive that makes it to the very crown of the Pharaoh who in Egypt was thought of as incarnation of God.*
*Snakes, that shed skins as if reborn, have been long interpreted as a symbol of death and rebirth, and so eternity and the cosmos in many cultures throughout the world.*
*The world is supported on the backs of four elephants, with a giant snake eating her own tail coiling around it, in Hindu mythology.*
*In Norse mythology, the giant sea serpent Jormungand coils around the seas of the world, grasping his own tail in his mouth.*
*Even the deity local to Central America, Quetzalcoatl, is sometimes found pictured as a winged snake eating its own tail.*
*Ancient Greece was greatly influenced by Egyptian culture, and many of its philosophers — among them Plato — took considerable interest in Ouroboros.*
*In Gnosticism, which took root in antique philosophy, a serpent biting its tail symbolized eternity and the soul of the world.*
*There has been found a Greek papyrus on alchemy that has a drawing of Ouroboros.*
*Half of its body is painted in white, half in black — representing Gnostic duality.*
*In alchemy, it is a symbol of order (cosmos) that is at odds with the primordial world of chaos. Ouroboros is also sometimes used to symbolize androgyny, fertility, and self-fertilization.*
*Gnosticism was a prominent heretical movement of the second century Christian Church, partly of pre-Christian (Jewish) origin.*
*It mainly concentrated on answering the question of why evil and pain existed in a world supposedly created by an omnipotent benevolent being.*
*Judaism explained evil as something caused by the fallen angels that defied and acted against the will of God; Christianity inherited this belief as well.*
*Gnosticism, however, interprets this world as a creation of a lesser divinity, the demiurge, that is already inherently evil.*
*Divine beings, taking the place of angels in Gnosticism, are called Aeons.*
*Meaning "having knowledge" in Ancient Greek, Gnosticism is a tool to give the abstract love and truth that leaks to this world from the one absolute benevolent God — Monad — physical shape.*
*Before the birth of the world, there existed an incarnation of knowledge in the supreme divine realm of Pleroma — Aeon Pistis Sophia.*
*Sophia, the feminine aspect of God, and the youngest of the Aeons, in her foolishness desiring to create something apart from the divine totality, gave birth to a child through the abortive act of separate creation.*
*This was how Demiurge, the fake creator God has been born.*
*This creator God is visualized in many different ways in Gnosticism. In the Gnosticism scripture "Hypostasis of the Archons" he is described as a blind god, and likened to Samael.*
*In "Pistis Sophia" he is likened to the archangel Ariel "Lion of God" that makes an appearance in the apocrypha "Book of Ezra."*
*He is probably best known from the "Apocryphon of John" where he appears as Yaldabaoth (the true meaning of the name is still a subject of discussion, but many scholars believe it to come from the Hebrew words "son of chaos").*
*In the Valentinian literature, Sophia had separated her feelings for her father (the Monad) in the form of Achamoth, that in turn molded Yaldabaoth as another Aeon into the Pleroma.*
*Yaldabaoth is usually depicted as a lion and snake, or a dragon reminiscent of a lion, who could have pillars of fire erupt from his eyes.*
*The fake god had many faces, and could take the shape of whatever his heart desired.*
*Seeing her son's terrifying appearance, Pistis Sophia realizes her foolishness, and expels Yaldabaoth from Pleroma.*
*Still, despite being a foolish being Yaldabaoth had inherited a part of the Monad's powers through his mother, and uses them to create many other Aeons.*
*Those Aeons grew to be known Archons (ruler in Greek).*
*They then created the seven layers of Heaven with Yaldabaoth to rule on the top, the abyss of boundless chaos down below, and, in the image of the true God they saw reflected in water, Adam, the first man.*
*Still, even the combined strength of Archons wasn't enough to fill Adam with life and make him move.*
*Sophia, regretting her mistake, asks the absolute God for pity, and fills Adam with the divine light of knowledge and truth, that gives him soul and life, finally allowing him to move.*
*Growing jealous of Adam, Yaldabaoth from then on locks the otherwise divine and transcendent nature of humans into the prison of flesh, and keeps causing them harm for all time to come.*
*According to The Apocryphon of John, after exiling Adam from paradise, Yaldabaoth rapes Eve, and haves her give birth to the unrighteous YHWH and the righteous Elohim both bearing the faces of bears.*
*These two then end up taking the roles of Cain and Abel, as the first murderer and the first victim in the world.*
*The primordial goddess of the ocean in Mesopotamian Religion.*
*Her name meaning "bitter water," she symbolized the waters of the primordial sea of chaos that slumbered there before the creation of the world.*
*She mated with Apsu "sweet water" or, in other words, "fresh water" and gave birth to many children.*
*According to Babylonian creation mythos "Enuma Elis," she was a monster with her upper body that of a woman, and lower body that of a snake.*
*Tiamat and Apsu had a son named Ea, that is thought to have evolved into the concept of Jewish and Christian God who used to be called "El."*
*At one time, unable to sleep and angered by the noise and commotion caused by his son, Apsu asks Tiamat to kill him.*
*While Tiamat has more than enough power to perform the deed, she refused out of the affection for her children. Meanwhile, learning of the plot, Ea, together with other young gods, use a spell on Apsu to imprison him in a deathlike state of sleep.*
*In the end, Tiamat doesn't interfere with the ploys of her children, but as next Marduk, Ea's son, interferes with her own slumber, she finally takes a stand for herself.*
*Marduk was originally a fertility god local to Babylonia in southern Mesopotamia, but as Babylon became the center of the Mesopotamian culture, he was elevated to the top of their pantheon.*
*Maduk had four eyes, so seeing everything, and four ears, so hearing everything.*
*Rising taller than any other god, even Ea is impressed by his son's splendor, presenting him with the gift of four winds of the world.*
*However, Marduk's playing with the wind ends up stirring trouble on the salty seas and enraging the old gods. Tiamat decides to kill her grandson for his insolence.*
*She, and her new husband Kingu, give birth to an army of monsters including of Basmu ("Venomous Snake"), Usumgallu ("Great Dragon"), Mushussu ("Furious Snake"), Lahmu (the "Hairy One"), Uridimmu ("Mad Lion"), Girtablullu ("Scorpion-Man"), and Kusarikku ("Bull-Man").*
*The gods are frightened at the prospect of facing this army, but then Marduk steps up.*
*Marduk offers to fight Tiamat in exchange for being made the absolute king of the gods, and faces her armed with a mace, a bow and arrows, a net, and seven winds.*
*Destroying the army led by Kingu alone, he catches Tiamat in a net, and has seven winds fill her body with air like a balloon.*
*He then shoots an arrow into her mouth that pierces her heart, killing her.*
*Marduk then splits Tiamat's body into two, making heaven and earth of each half.*
*He buries her head under a mountain and pierces her eyes, which become the sources for the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.*
*There are, however, more curious literature regarding Tiamat.*
*In 1977 Schlangekraft, Inc. published an "English translation" of a grimoire named Simon Necronomicon (named after the man who allegedly writes its introduction) that was said to have originally been in the possession of the theologian Montague Summers in Greek language.*
*Necronomicon is a fictitious book that was said to contain the truth of ancient deranged beings "The Old Ones" creating the world and living beings on a whim, that figures in the works of an American horror writer H.P. Lovecraft.*
*The prologue of the Simon Necronomicon explains how a Mad Arab Abdul Alhazred first came to discover the dark secrets that he is recording.*
*He accidentally witnesses an arcane ritual performed by a cult that worships Tiamat.*
*Both the demons C'thulhu and Humbaba (a forest monster that is slayed by the heroes Gilgamesh and Enkidu in the Babylonian folklore) are conjured.*
*Tiamat is listed among the Elder Gods in the book, and even Marduk makes an appearance as an "Old God" that opposes them.*
*According to the Simon Necronomicon, you have to sacrifice eleven men to summon the elder god of chaos, Tiamat.*
